doctrine.master_principle: Posing is the photographer's responsibility, not the subject's. The photographer bears full accountability for bringing out the subject's best form across all body types, contexts, and experience levels. Confidence on-set is the single highest-leverage variable: photographer energy transfers directly to subject energy, which determines expression quality.
three_phase_posing_structure: Phase 1 - Mechanical: Set spine alignment, weight distribution, body angle, and limb placement. This is the structural skeleton. Establish before anything else.
Phase 2 - Movement: Direct controlled motion (walk, sway, turn, interact). Movement adjusts body naturally and creates expression conditions. Static = dead. Movement creates liveliness.
Phase 3 - Expression capture: Shoot at the expression parabola peaks (before apex and right after descent, not at peak itself). Use 10-12 fps burst when prompting for expression.
session_sequence: Step 1: Pre-shoot insecurity audit. Ask subjects about body parts they want minimized or emphasized. Design pose menu accordingly before first frame.
Step 2: Assess attire. Heavy/bulky gowns limit movement poses. Form-fitting enables romantic walk and dynamic sequences.
Step 3: Read the light. Identify light source direction before starting. Body angle follows light (away from light, face toward light).
Step 4: Assess subject experience. Inexperienced subjects need direct mechanical posing. Experienced subjects need prompted freedom; micromanagement kills them.
Step 5: Warm up. Demo movements. Use mirroring method: demonstrate first, subject copies. Breaks formal photography taboo and creates psychological permission to move.
Step 6: Lock classic safe shots first (roughly 40% of session). Clean, on-camera, clear deliverables. This makes remaining time expendable for creative risk.
Step 7: Execute creative/movement poses (roughly 60%) once safe shots are confirmed.
Step 8: Multiply variations before moving to new pose. Five core poses executed well with 10 variations each yields 50+ solid images. Master depth-of-pose before breadth-of-pose.

weight_distribution: Universal female foundation: shift weight onto back hip/leg. Almost all flattering female poses are built on this single principle first, then angle/arm/expression layered on top.
Never stand flatfooted (penguin posture). Always create diagonal angle between feet.
One leg always in front of the other. Diagonal angles slim appearance vs square-on stance.
When seated: tilt knees diagonally, not straight at camera.
body_angle: 45-degree angle principle: body 45 degrees away from light source until shadow appears at center of garment; face and toe angle toward camera/light.
Female form: turn body away from light, emphasize curves with chest forward, arms off body.
Male form: turn toward light source to create V-shape and appear broader. Lean forward (chest/shoulders toward camera, gut back) to create valleys and peaks.
Rotation principle: rotating subject slightly on any existing pose creates an entirely new image instantly. Use as efficiency multiplier when stuck.
chin_and_jaw: Turtle technique: extend neck forward and down (chin forward, not inward). Feels awkward, looks sharp. Elongates jawline and smooths under-chin.
Chin direction creates connection energy: lean chins toward each other in couple posing and the body naturally adjusts, creating intimacy without explicit instruction.
Elevated camera angle assists double chin mitigation. Forward chin + slightly high camera angle = ideal.
For tight frames: chin to shoulder creates feminine energy when executed correctly.
arms_and_hands: Gap between arm and body is mandatory for women. Pressing arms flat to body widens them. Pull elbows back or bend arms to create gap.
Asymmetry beats symmetry. Asymmetrical hand placement looks intentional; symmetrical looks posed.

Hand engagement menu: holding hair, holding veil, hand on hip at narrowest point, hands in pockets (thumbs visible, not fully hidden), hands on biceps, one hand active + one passive, gripping fabric or prop.
Men: one hand active (holding jacket, adjusting watch, gripping cuff), one hand in pocket (full hand for dress pants, fingertips only in jeans, thumb down not horizontal). Never frame crotch.
Finger wave position: raise fingers like a staircase for visual interest and light variation.
Static hands are awkward. Always give hands a deliberate job.
Negative space triangles: arm bends and hand positions that create gaps make subjects look taller and leaner.
shoulders_and_posture: Drop one shoulder more than the other. Asymmetric shoulder placement reads as elegant; symmetric reads as cheerful.
String posture cue: imagine string at base of spine pulling upward. Proprioceptive not verbal. Prevents slouching at odd angles.
Men: shoulders down and braced, chest forward, elbow gap creating air triangle between armpit and hip.
Shrug shoulders up then release to reset tension and find natural resting position.
Belly management: tighten abdominal as if doing a gym crunch, not aggressive suck-in. Maintains natural appearance.
feet_and_legs: Heel off ground activates leg line. Cross legs for gap between knees.
Never pigeon-toed. Point toes outward or forward.
Foot positioning: never in painful-looking position (pain reads in the photo).
Short people: low angles always (shoot up from below to increase perceived height). Half-body crop preferred.
Men: feet shoulder-width or slightly narrower, bend front knee slightly, weight on back leg.

female: S-curve body: ankles together or crossed, lift one heel, collapse that knee inward, turn hip away from camera. Creates thinning silhouette.
Curve emphasis: shoulders back, lean chest forward, hand on waist at narrowest point.
Breathing technique: brief inhale before shot tightens and fills bust area naturally.
Smise: smile without teeth (solution for tooth insecurity). Eyes engaged, mouth closed.
Arms off body creates slim arm appearance. Counterintuitive but essential.
Three expression tiers to cycle: cool/magazine smolder, soft/painting gentle, fun/laughing authentic.
Golden angle: each person has an optimal facial profile. Test multiple chin and head angles to find it.
Camera angle: petite women benefit from slightly-below-waist angle to lengthen legs. Avoid shooting down on short subjects.
male: Goal psychology: men want to look cool and commanding, not sexy. Frame direction accordingly.
V-shape framing: turn toward light, elbows out creating air triangle at armpit, chest forward, gut back. Creates width and authority.
Lean-forward posture is intentional strength (glorified slouch). Concave upper body creates valleys and peaks.
Avoid over-posing. Excess emotionality or feminine angle (body away from light, chin to outer shoulder) makes masculine pose read feminine.
If waist looks broad: rotate 15 degrees toward camera to narrow the visible width.
Thumb rule: thumbs IN pockets, never pointing horizontal (crude read).
Props give hands activity: watch adjustment, jacket hold, cufflink touch, prop surface to lean on.
couples: Groom as conversation engine: groom already knows partner's laugh triggers. Direct groom to lead interaction. Removes photographer from needing to amuse couple.
Task couple to talk and interact continuously. Continuous conversation prevents self-consciousness.
Whisper prompt: direct groom to whisper in bride's ear while bride looks to a distant point. Reliably evokes genuine laughter.
Cognitive overload for candid: give too many sequential directions (walk, push, twirl, dance, hug, sway) and subject stops self-monitoring. Natural candid results.
Directorial posing: direct couple to repeat same general action while photographer changes angle and zoom. Multiple distinct looks from one choreographed sequence.
Lipstare: foreheads close, both staring at each other's lips. Precursor to natural kiss. Bride holds back of groom's head, groom holds bride's waist.

plus_size: Emotion and expression override body visibility. Joy, laughter, and movement read stronger than body awareness.
Partial blocking: use props, objects, or hands carrying items to obscure strategically.
Half-body framing with strong expression outperforms full-body with average expression.
Never shoot square at torso. Always 45 degrees or more.
Side lighting creates contour shadow. Diffused light reduces highlighting.
High-energy action poses (dancing, moving) distract from shape.
thin: Avoid full frontal square stance, side-profile single angle, or low angles (accentuate thinness).
Layer clothing for visual bulk. Use accessories: belts, watches, glasses.
Props give physical presence: guitar, chair, structural surface.
Negative space triangles from arm angles and leg spacing create visual bulk.
Broad-lit (light on wider side of face) increases perceived mass. Good for thin male subjects.
Face-forward square poses and eye-level or slightly high angles work better than angular approaches.
short: Shoot from low angles (below subject, angled up) always.
Half-body crop preferred. Full-body shows proportion gaps.
Avoid scale props (bikes, cars) that emphasize size difference.
High or eye-level camera angle only, never shoot from above.
Background without comparative scale elements (walls, blank backgrounds) remove size reference.
tall: Full-body shots are an asset. Lean into them.
Higher camera angles work better than below angles.
Can carry more complex poses and more prominent props without scale issues.

lighting_posing_integration: Short-lit (light on narrow side of face): narrows face appearance. Use for wider faces or subjects wanting to appear thinner.
Broad-lit (light on wider side of face): increases perceived mass. Use for thin male subjects.
Body direction follows light: body away from light source, face turns toward it.
Lighting responsibility for darker skin tones: use light meter for precise exposure. Never let darker skin fade into darkness.
Background management: use aperture priority, small f-stop (f/1.4 to f/2.8), zoom to maximum, focus on face/eyes to separate subject from environment.
Rule of thirds: subject left or right third, face on top third line. Frame interesting background elements on third lines.
confidence_and_on_set_energy: Confidence is the primary posing tool. Nervous photographer produces stiff photos regardless of technical placement.
Voice energy transfers directly: flat low-energy voice produces flat stiff expressions. Speak with rhythm and energy.
Shutter sound as psychological anchor: audible mechanical shutter confirms to subject that photographer is working. Silent mode subconsciously signals failure or inactivity. Do not switch to silent.
Never use negative directives: instead of 'don't do that,' say 'let's try this' while demonstrating the correction.
Personal energy management is professional work, not secondary concern.
Monitor spine continuously: posture slouches within 10 seconds of setting a static pose. Continuous observation required.
expression_tactics: Expression parabola timing: best expressions occur right before peak and right after descent, not at the peak itself. Burst mode at 10-12 fps eliminates timing guesswork.
Three expression tiers: cool/smolder (magazine), soft/gentle (painting), fun/authentic (laughing). Cycle through all three per session.
Avoid dead/stiff expressions by directing gaze off-camera or to a specific point. Direct gaze requires present expression/energy to avoid empty stare.
Never stop moving: continuous motion produces better candid moments than static posing.

Inner diversity concept: challenge subject's self-limiting beliefs about what versions of themselves are accessible (sexy, cool, sensual, powerful). Reframes posing as identity exploration not performance.
named_pose_library: Body to Body: couple face each other, groom holds bride's waist, continuous talking/interaction.
Car Lean: groom leans on vehicle, bride sandwiches him, couple keeps talking.
King on the Throne: groom sits authoritatively, bride stands beside with body angled to flatter gown.
Whisper Sweet Nothings: bride looks to a distant point, groom whispers in her ear. Reliably evokes genuine reaction.
Hero Bride: groom soft-focused in background admiring, bride front-and-center showcasing gown.
Horizon Pose: couple holds hands or waist, groom gestures toward far horizon. Romantic future-looking framing.
The Leader: groom at front leading, bride follows. Power dynamic pose.
Lipstare: foreheads close, both staring at each other's lips. Precursor to natural kiss.
Love Story / Multi-Exposure: tripod-mounted, multiple positions stacked in post at reduced opacity. Narrative arc in single frame.
Romantic Walk: couple holds hands, walks while talking (not looking at camera). Avoid with heavy gowns.
Spanish Guitar: groom holds bride like guitar, she falls back looking at him. Not for plus-size couples.
Spoon: groom stands behind bride whispering or kissing shoulder. Both facing same direction, relaxed.
Titanic: couple at elevation, bride opens to world, groom protective from behind.
Hand on Biceps with Wrist Roll: feminine bend, looks elegant. Lady boss energy.
Hands on Hair: excuse for arms off body. Bent arms, legs crossed.
Smise: closed-mouth smile with engaged eyes. Use for tooth insecurity.
Dip: groom dips bride backward, wide stable stance, bride extends one leg pointed, bouquet faces camera.
Sushi Roll: couple holds hands out wide, spins, rocks back-and-forth. Playful motion trigger.
Swing Dress: bride swings dress in circular motion. Movement capture.
Foreheads Together: noses close, forehead to forehead. Intimacy without kiss.
Back-to-Back Lean: lean back against each other, one leg popped, both toward camera.
Sitting Between Legs: one partner between other's legs facing forward.
Spinal Correction Lean: use structural element (wall, ladder, chair) to create prop-supported pose that gives hands and legs natural activity.

pre_shoot_gates: Insecurity audit: identify body parts subject wants minimized or emphasized before designing pose sequence.
Attire check: assess gown weight and fit before confirming which poses are feasible.
Light confirmation: identify light source direction before starting.
Body composition read: note height differences or body type variations that affect pose selection.
Couple connection level: assess comfort to determine if intimate poses need warm-up or are accessible immediately.
Experience level check: experienced subjects need prompted freedom; inexperienced need direct mechanical direction.
Frame constraint lock: decide full-body vs half-body vs close-up framing before adding pose complexity.
Time constraint acknowledgment: in time-pressured situations, stick to 3-4 repeatable poses across 2-3 locations.

acceptable_if_expression_is_strong: Finger awkwardness or minor hand placement imperfection
Small shoulder asymmetry off from ideal
requires_immediate_reset: Full elbow visibly awkward or pointing at wrong angle
Hands at creepy or unnatural angles
T-Rex effect (200mm lens compresses raised arm into stubby proportion)

technical_tools: 10-12 fps burst mode: expression timing capture at parabola peaks
Mechanical shutter with audible feedback: psychological anchor for subject confidence
Light meter: precise exposure for darker skin tones
Tripod (6ft minimum): multi-exposure compositing and self-portrait work
Bluetooth remote clicker: essential for solo self-portrait shooting
Aperture priority mode, smallest f-stop (f/1.4 to f/2.8), zoom to maximum: background separation
V-flat reflector: shadow control and fill
Props: chairs, ladders, vehicles, veils, bouquets, watches, jackets, belts
Pinterest: idea reference only, never session script (kills on-set creativity)
weird_gold: Chin-lean as connection trigger: just directing 'lean your chin toward each other' adjusts the whole body naturally and creates intimacy without explicit full-body instruction.
Expression parabola: peak is too much; before and after are the usable frames. Burst mode eliminates the guesswork of timing.
Cognitive overload for candid: give too many sequential actions and subject stops self-monitoring. Accidentally natural.
Shutter sound as psychological anchor: silent mode subconsciously communicates nothing is happening, kills vulnerability.
Groom as conversation engine: grooms know their partner's laugh triggers. The photographer does not need to be funny; the groom does.
Safe shots enable creative risk: knowing classics are locked makes remaining shots expendable, which is what enables bravery.
Back-hip weight shift as universal foundation: nearly all flattering female poses descend from one principle. Simplifies coaching dramatically.
String cue is proprioceptive not verbal: subjects can't 'hear' their way into posture but they can feel a pull from the base of their spine.
T-Rex effect is lens compression, not pose failure: 200mm + raised arm toward camera = stubby arm in frame. Awareness of focal length changes entire framing strategy.
Voice energy is the actual subject: flat voice produces stiff faces even when hand placement is perfect. The photographer's internal state is the session.
Insecurity-aware pose design: knowing what the subject wants to minimize before shooting allows clinical design of a pose menu that prevents the problem rather than correcting mid-session.
Rotation as infinite multiplier: any pose becomes a different image with minor rotation. Velocity tool when creative momentum slows.
Thumb position disproportionate impact: thumbs-in-pockets vs horizontal changes entire frame read from formal to crude. Fraction of an inch of placement matters.
Inner diversity reframe: 'you contain all versions of yourself' changes posing from external performance to internal identity access. Lowers resistance dramatically.
contradictions_resolved: Symmetry for baseline vs asymmetry for elegance: asymmetric arm/leg placement over a symmetric structural core. Asymmetry lives in the limbs, not the spine.

Over-posing makes men look feminine vs men require intentional posing: excessive emotionality and feminine angle (body away from light, chin to outer shoulder) cause the feminine read, not the act of posing itself.
Micromanagement vs freedom: experienced subjects need freedom (prompting), inexperienced need direct instruction (posing). Same instruction style fails if not audience-adapted.
Classic poses as required vs cliche: classics are required deliverables and confidence baseline. Creativity overlays on top; replacing classics entirely makes the session directionless.
Emotion-first vs pose-first: poses are the structural framework; emotion is the content filling that framework. The system enables emotion rather than replacing it.

Movement is better vs movement causes mistakes: acceptable mistakes from movement are preferable if expression is strong. Unacceptable mistakes (T-Rex, neck collapse) require reset regardless of expression.

notes: Source is a 23-segment transcript corpus from 7+ distinct instructional voices (Tim Shields, Sal Cincotta, Omar Gonzalez, Valenzuela, Cassidy, Gress, Oscar Ntege, Joseph Radhik, and others). Junk density ranges from low in segments 1-10 to approximately 60% in segments 11-20 (conference promotion, instructor bios, filler). All real operative doctrine has been extracted, deduplicated, and cross-referenced. Named pose library reflects segments 21-23 primarily. Three-phase structure and confidence doctrine reflect segments 11-20 primarily. Body-type mechanics and foundational recipes reflect segments 1-10 primarily. The consolidated doctrine supersedes all three partial segment files.
